newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr edges ahead in hope of budget relief.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr edges ahead in hope of budget relief.

text.p: The Australian dollar crept higher in its all too familiar range Tuesday with dealers reporting offshore bids from widespread sources in good two-way trade.

Japanese and U.S. banks were amongst the buyers while Swiss names were on either side as the currency slowly gathered a 1/3 cent of gains. A steadier US$/yen and a retreat in the mark helped it recoup some losses on the crosses, while a rise in base metal and oil prices drew demand from U.S. commodity funds.
There was also an expectation the Federal 1997/98 Budget, to be handed down at 7.30 pm, would ensure Australia was one of the few industrialised economies without a huge budget deficit.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local dollar had advanced to US$0.7814/19 from an early US$0.7789/94 and US$0.7775/80 late here Monday.

The rise still left it in the no-man's land of the US$0.7720/7860 range held for more than a month now and analysts emphasised it would have to clear US$0.7835 at least to put momentum in an otherwise directionless chart outlook.

Weeks of aimless wandering had also left a tangled web of support and resistance levels including US$0.7775, US$0.7735 and US$0.7720 on the downside while US$0.7825, US$0.7835 and US$0.7860 were all seen as major barriers.
On the crosses the currency edged up to 93.15/25 yen from and early 92.83/93 and Monday's late 92.41/51, but was still far below the lofty 99.00 level held early last week.

Sentiment was steadied somewhat by a rally, albeit modest, in US$/yen as the market reacted to more calming words from Japanese officials. In particular, a top Bank of Japan official said the bank needed more time to assess the economic outlook, a statement analysts took as an attempt to hose down speculation of an imminent hike in interest rates.
That helped the U.S. dollar steady at 119.25/30 after being as low as 118.75 at one stage this morning.
The local dollar also regained ground on a broadly softer mark to stand at 1.3300/10 from 1.3121/35 late here Monday and rallied to 59.9 in trade weighted terms from 59.5.
On the domestic front, the Federal Budget has not had much fanfare in the markets but still promises to cement the fiscal improvement set in place by the tight budget of 1996/97.

Median expectations are the government will cut between A$1.5-2.0 billion from the underlying deficit for 1997/98 leaving a shortfall of around A$2.0 billion. The headline balance will be in surplus by around A$10 billion, thanks to privatisation receipts so there should be no net bond issuance.

Analysts expect the government to forecast a balanced underlying budget for 1998/99 or maybe even a small surplus. That would be an impressive performance compared to much of the OECD and could take Australia a step closer to earning a credit upgrade for its foreign debt.

There were some concerns the Treasurer might rely too much on ambitious economic assumptions rather than proper spending and taxation measures and analysts warned a GDP growth forecast above 4.0 percent would quickly draw accusations of fudging.
Underlying inflation was likely to be estimated at around 2.5 percent, much in line with the Reserve Bank's thinking.
For the dollar, a tight budget would not always be bullish since it might also be taken as providing scope for an easing in monetary policy.
But in this case the Reserve Bank only last week said it saw no economic benefit in another rate cut and implied it had already taken the likely budget outcome into account in its deliberations.
Given that, and assuming the budget did not disappoint in its fiscal credentials, dealers expected it be supportive of both Australian bonds and the dollar in the longer term.
